catalog_quote: There are two patterns of stress placement depending on the morphological structure of the word. Stress placement on monomorphemic words is phonological conditioned and predictable. Stress placement on polymorphemic words (i.e. verbs and possessed nouns is grammatically conditioned and predictable but to a lesser degree than for monomorphemic words. For monomorphemic words stress falls on the first closed syllable, which is usually though not necessary the last syllable in the word, or if there is no closed syllable, then on the first syllable. For the purpose of stress placement an off-glide functions as a closed syllable when it occurs in word final position. For polymorphemic words grammatical factors play a greater role then phonological factors. With the inalienable possessed nouns there is a general stress rule whereby main stress is placed on the final syllable of the word. With the verbs stress placement can be placed on any of the following elements depending on the particular conjugation of the verb: the subject agreement suffix, the aspectual/mood/negative marker, the infinitive clitic or the object marker. [...] First closed syllable: [du.ˈɑn] ‘cold’; [gɑ.Ɂɑ.ˈlit] ‘small plant’; [ɑ.ˈgin.Ɂɑi] ‘sticky’; [ˈlɛs.ɑ.lɛs] ‘type of grass’. Vowel glide functioning as closed syllable: [fu.ˈɑu] ‘red ant’; [hɑ.Ɂi.ˈsɑi] ‘where?’. First syllable: [ˈgɑ.gɑ.tu] ‘darkness’; [ˈsɑ.gi.gi.li] ‘feeling of sickness’. Inalienable possessed nouns: [o.lɑ.ˈni] ‘my face’.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Monomorphemic words: stress the first (leftmost) closed syllable (CVC, or word-final vowel+off-glide), e.g. [du.'an] 'cold', [ga.?a.'lit] 'small plant', ['les.a.les] 'grass sp.'; if the word has no closed syllable, stress the first syllable (['ga.ga.tu] 'darkness', ['sa.gi.gi.li]). So placement is quantity/closure-sensitive with a default-to-initial. Polymorphemic words are grammatically conditioned: inalienably possessed nouns take final stress ([o.la.'ni] 'my face'); verbs stress a particular suffix/clitic (subject agreement, aspect/mood/negative marker, infinitive clitic =ec/oc, or object marker) depending on the conjugation.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed (only 'main stress' mentioned for possessed nouns; no secondary stress marked in examples).
new_statements.exceptions: Polymorphemic words (verbs, inalienably possessed nouns) follow morphological rules rather than the closed-syllable rule; verbs' stress site varies by conjugation and is 'predictable but to a lesser degree'. 'usually though not necessary the last syllable' notes that the first closed syllable need not be final.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level stress on citation forms; author distinguishes monomorphemic (phonologically conditioned) vs polymorphemic (grammatically conditioned) words. No tone or contrastive length reported in the section.
new_statements.identity_note: Source describes Bau [bbd] = Glottolog bauu1244 as a whole (villages Bau, Bafulo/Dae, Guman, Gumaru, Efu, Fulumu, Bamahal, Dolonu, Lagaha, Bauk; pop. 3142, census 2000); no dialect restriction stated. Classification given in the source: TNG, Madang-Adelbert Range, Mabuso Stock, Gum (Abaian) family.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Monomorphemic words: stress the first closed (CVC) syllable of the word, a word-final vowel + off-glide counting as closed; if the word has no closed syllable, stress the first syllable. Examples p. 7-8: [du.'an] 'cold', [ga.?a.'lit] 'small plant', [a.'gin.?ai] 'sticky', ['les.a.les] 'type of grass', [fu.'au] 'red ant', [ha.?i.'sai] 'where?', ['ga.ga.tu] 'darkness', ['sa.gi.gi.li] 'feeling of sickness'. Polymorphemic words are grammatically conditioned: inalienably possessed nouns stress the final syllable ([ga.ti.'na.ga] 'their heads', [o.la.'ni] 'my face', [wa.'?u] 'his stomach'); verbs stress the subject-agreement suffix, the aspectual/mood/negative marker, the infinitive clitic or the object marker depending on the conjugation (examples p. 8).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned; only main stress ('main stress' named once, for possessed nouns) is marked.
new_statements.exceptions: Polymorphemic words (verbs, inalienably possessed nouns) follow morphological rather than phonological rules and are 'predictable but to a lesser degree'; the placement in verbs depends on the particular conjugation (subject-agreement suffix / aspect-mood-negative marker / infinitive clitic / object marker). No tone or length contrast is described in the section despite its title.
new_statements.identity_note: Van der Meer 2008 p. 1 identifies the variety as Bau (BBD), Madang, Mabuso Stock, Gum (Abaian) family; major villages Bau, Bafulo/Dae, Guman, Gumaru, Efu, Fulumu, Bamahal, Dolonu, Lagaha, Bauk. No dialect is singled out; the 1976 Gasaway & Sims manuscript cited in its bibliography (p. 12) is titled 'Fulumu (Bau)', i.e. the Fulumu village variety, but that manuscript is unpublished and was not seen.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Monomorphemic words: stress the first closed syllable of the word (a word-final vowel+off-glide counts as closed), wherever it is ([du.'an], [ga.?a.'lit], [a.'gin.?ai], ['les.a.les], [fu.'au]); if no syllable is closed, stress the first syllable (['ga.ga.tu], ['sa.gi.gi.li]). Polymorphemic words are morphologically conditioned: inalienably possessed nouns stress the word-final syllable ([o.la.'ni], [wa.'?u]); verbs stress the subject-agreement suffix, the aspect/mood/negative marker, the infinitive clitic or the object marker depending on the conjugation (examples PDF p. 8). No tone or contrastive length is described.
new_statements.secondary_stress: none described (only 'main stress' is mentioned, for possessed nouns; no secondary marks in the transcriptions)
new_statements.exceptions: Polymorphemic words (verbs, inalienably possessed nouns) follow grammatical, not phonological, placement and are 'predictable but to a lesser degree'; word-final off-glides count as closed syllables.
new_statements.identity_note: Bau (BBD), Madang Province; Mabuso Stock, Gum (Abaian) family; villages Bau, Bafulo/Dae, Guman, Gumaru, Efu, Fulumu, Bamahal, Dolonu, Lagaha, Bauk (2008 OPD p. 1); older SIL name Fulumu (Gasaway & Sims 1976). No dialect differentiation is made in the OPD.
